extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics and general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical guidance and evaluative criteria for judging English poets and their works (style, authenticity, subject, imagination vs reason, moral/contextual considerations), drawn from lecture-form criticism of major English poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of style / pruning redundances
rubrics_metrics.description: Akenside improved his Pleasures of the Imagination in subsequent editions by pruning away a great many redundances of style and ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove redundant phrases and ornamental excess; tighter expression improves poetic quality. (Example: later editions improved by pruning.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject (exhilaration/interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subjects are less exhilarating (example: Armstrong's choice of 'The Art of Preserving Health' is not very exhilarating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects that naturally engage the reader; dull or overly didactic topics risk uninspiring verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone and force for satirical/comic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Churchill's Satires are 'strong, coarse, and full of an air of hardened assurance' — the tone suits the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the strength, coarseness, or assurance of tone to the demands of satire or comic writing; inappropriate softness or mismatch dilutes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowing and elegant versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldsmith is described as 'the most flowing and elegant of our versifiers since Pope.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smooth, elegant metrical movement and ease of lineation are marks of high versification. Look for natural rhythm and sustained fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artless naturalness / unstudied manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldsmith has 'traits of artless nature ... manners unstudied, but a gentle heart' and performs 'miracles of skill from pure happiness of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unforced, unstudied expression and a natural grace often produce more charm than overt artifice; sincerity of manner is valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Felicity in turns of phrase and effective repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldsmith has 'a peculiar felicity in his turns upon words, which he constantly repeated with delightful effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful word-turns and judicious repetition can be delightful; repetition should feel purposeful and enhance effect rather than be mere habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of originality and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldsmith's genius was 'a mixture of originality and imitation: he could do nothing without some model before him, and he could copy nothing that he did not adorn with the graces of his own mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using models is acceptable provided the poet transforms or adorns what is borrowed with personal originality; slavish copying is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning should lead to interesting thought, not display
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more admirable than the learning displayed, or the inference that it is of no use but as it leads to interesting thought and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly learning in poetry should serve to illuminate ideas and prompt reflection rather than merely showcase erudition; avoid pedantry for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnets: virtue of brevity (but risk of being tedious)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sonnet 'has the necessary advantage of being short (though it is also sometimes both 'tedious and brief').' Warton wrote some of the finest sonnets treating pleasing subjects in a pleasing and philosophical way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sonnet's brevity to concentrate thought and feeling; avoid making a short form feel thin or tediously compressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate works independently of precocity/age
rubrics_metrics.description: The lists of fame are not filled with the dates of births or deaths; the side-mark of the age at which works were done wears out in works destined for immortality. Don't estimate genius primarily by prematureness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the intrinsic quality of compositions rather than being unduly impressed by the author's youth or circumstances of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticate historical language; watch for imposture
rubrics_metrics.description: Chatterton's supposed 'antique' poems read as smooth modern poems unless you pronounce the words as they were spoken at the time claimed; the secret of the imposture lies in repetition of obsolete words and the mis-spelling of common ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test claims of antiquity, check pronunciation, accentual patterns, orthography, and anachronistic fluency; inconsistency (modern smoothness with token 'obsolete' spellings) is a sign of forgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggerated, hyperbolic praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Some learned commentators raised Chatterton to extravagant heights ('greatest genius... second to Shakespeare'), producing progressively exaggerated descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of escalating superlatives that conflate enthusiasm with evidence; base judgments on concrete qualities of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and simplicity over artificial poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns 'did not create a soul ... by tinkling siren sounds, or by piling up centos of poetic diction; but for the artificial flowers of poetry, he plucked the mountain-daisy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct, authentic language and simple natural imagery to ornate, learned, or composite poetic diction that feels manufactured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groundedness in life; authenticity from lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns 'held the plough or the pen with the same firm, manly grasp' and used everyday life (a field-mouse, a mountain-daisy) as poetic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry grounded in concrete lived experience often carries conviction and vitality; connection to real life enriches depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness vs sickly sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns 'was not a sickly sentimentalist ... a namby-pamby poet, a mincing metre ballad-monger' — he had 'the same life of mind' and 'as much of a man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mawkishness or over-delicate sentiment; healthy, robust feeling and directness often serve comic or social verse better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful depiction of social life, humour, and local customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns's 'pictures of good fellowship, of social glee, of quaint humour' are 'equal to anything ... come up to nature, and they cannot go beyond it.' Halloween is 'the most striking and picturesque description of local customs and scenery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid, faithful rendering of manners, customs, and humour lends authority and appeal to poetry; local colour can be a major strength when true to life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-revelation: frankness and truth of description
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns 'has made us as well acquainted with himself as it is possible to be; has let out the honest impulses of his native disposition, the unequal conflict of the passions in his breast, with the same frankness and truth of description.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open, candid personal voice and truthful depiction of inner conflict can be a virtue; honest self-revelation often deepens readers' engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish moral character from poetic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been usual to attack Burns's moral character and the moral tendency of his writings at the same time; critics should not conflate the poet's private morals with his poetic achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the moral tendency of a work on its own terms and separate evaluation of artistic merit from moral censure of the author's life unless the text itself warrants condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's office: imagination over cool calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding exhibits things in their relative proportions and ultimate consequences; the imagination insists on immediate impressions and indulges strongest impulses; it is the poet's office to pamper the imagination of his readers and his own with the extremes of present ecstasy or agony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry often prioritizes immediate impression, emotional intensity, and imaginative excess rather than sober, prosaic analysis; evaluate poets by their success in creating powerful imaginative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that genius entails practical imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: All men of genius ... are liable to practical errors, from the very confidence their superiority inspires; poets are men of stronger imagination and keener sensibilities — too much to expect them to be distinguished only by sang-froid, circumspection, and sobriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should temper moral expectations of poets and recognize that exceptional imaginative gifts may coexist with practical or moral failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize faults by socio-economic pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns's habit of ale-house tippling or conjugal infidelities can be traced to struggles with fortune and the opposite calls of business and fancy (the incompatibility between the Muses and the Excise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account the poet's social and economic circumstances when explaining faults or behavior; context may mitigate or explain certain shortcomings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of comic/convivial writing often requires lived practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines depicting excesses of mirth and convivial indulgence (e.g. from Tam o' Shanter) could hardly have been written without the poet having 'drunk full often of the ton' — the act and practique part of life being the mistress of theorique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real familiarity with practices being described (drinking, conviviality, local rituals) lends credence and vividness to comic or social scenes; secondhand imitation may ring false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic writing should be agreeable chit-chat rather than pompous lecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldsmith's moral Essays in the Citizen of the World are 'as agreeable chit-chat as can be conveyed in the form of didactic discourses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing didactic or moral pieces, favor an engaging conversational tone over pompous didacticism to retain reader interest.
